skills.name: Angular
skills.note: Signals and standalone components made this genuinely pleasant. Zoneless removes the last piece of magic I could never fully explain to a reviewer.

skills.name: Java
skills.note: The language I reach for when a system has to still be correct in two years. Records, sealed types and pattern matching removed most of the ceremony that used to make Java tedious.

skills.name: Spring Boot
skills.note: Where most of my backend work lives. Constructor injection on final fields, one exception advice, and configuration that fails loudly at startup rather than quietly at 3am.

skills.name: TypeScript
skills.note: Strict mode from the first commit. The type system is the cheapest test suite there is, and the only one that runs on every keystroke.

skills.name: LLMs & RAG
skills.note: Retrieval that cites its sources, and tool definitions treated as untrusted input. Most of the failure modes are prompt-shaped, not model-shaped.

skills.name: PostgreSQL
skills.note: Row Level Security is the feature I underestimated longest. Getting the policies right means the database stays correct even when a client is wrong.

skills.name: Python
skills.note: For anything touching models, data or a quick proof. FastAPI when it needs an edge, a plain script when it does not.

skills.name: Docker
skills.note: Multi-stage builds, small final images, and a compose file so a new machine is running the stack in one command.

skills.name: Three.js
skills.note: Procedural geometry over downloaded models wherever possible. The cheapest asset is the one you generate at runtime.

skills.name: Flutter
skills.note: One codebase when a project genuinely needs to be on a phone, rather than because it sounded good in the plan.

extracurricular.title: Hackathons
extracurricular.blurb: Building something real in 36 hours, then defending it.
extracurricular.body: Where most of my projects started life. The constraint is the point: 36 hours forces you to decide what the thing actually is before you write a line of it.

extracurricular.title: Open Source
extracurricular.blurb: Publishing the tools rather than keeping them local.
extracurricular.body: GlyphGuard and the smaller utilities are public because a tool nobody can read is a tool nobody can trust. Writing the README properly usually improves the code.

extracurricular.title: Mentoring
extracurricular.blurb: Walking juniors through their first real codebase.
extracurricular.body: Mostly code review and pairing. Explaining why a boundary exists is the fastest way to find out whether it should.

extracurricular.title: College Tech Events
extracurricular.blurb: Organising and presenting at campus technical sessions.
extracurricular.body: Running the session is harder than speaking at it. Both taught me more about explaining a system than any amount of writing it did.

hobbies.title: Formula 1
hobbies.blurb: Strategy, telemetry, and arguing about pit windows.
hobbies.body: The reason PitLane AI exists. A race is a live optimisation problem with incomplete information — the closest thing in sport to a systems design interview.

hobbies.title: Anime
hobbies.blurb: Long-form stories that commit to their premise.
hobbies.body: Mostly the ones willing to be slow. MECCHA CHAMELEON came out of wanting to build something with that visual language rather than just watch it.

hobbies.title: Chess
hobbies.blurb: Losing on time in otherwise winning positions.
hobbies.body: Rapid, mostly. Useful practice at the thing engineering also demands: committing to a plan without full information, then adjusting when it stops being true.

hobbies.title: Music
hobbies.blurb: What is playing while the tests run.
hobbies.body: VibeMatch AI started here — the observation that what I actually want is a song with the same emotional shape, not the same genre tag.

blog.title: Why this portfolio looks like Netflix
blog.blurb: A catalogue is a better metaphor for a body of work than a list.
blog.body: A list of projects asks the reader to do the sorting. A catalogue does it for them: what is new, what is getting attention, what the author would pick. The rows are an argument about the work, not just a way to fit it on screen.

blog.title: The Supabase policy I got wrong
blog.blurb: SECURITY DEFINER functions were reachable over the public REST API.
blog.body: Row Level Security covered the tables, but the maintenance functions were SECURITY DEFINER and still granted to anon — reachable over PostgREST. The database linter caught it. Enabling RLS is not the same as being locked down.
